stage.description: Gary explains independent CP/M OEM availability, published interfaces and optional extensions; CP/M, hardware and application licenses remain distinct. MPI explains the printer partnership and any separately agreed future FlexiBUS devices. Do not announce the later July SMC agreement. The head of BPI Systems explains its independent brand, management, software ownership and support, with Adam investment and AION/Logix cooperation disclosed. No invented name or claim of unrelated ownership.

Show selected locations, first course dates and exact tuition once finalised. BPI-authorised courses and the dealer programme start July 17; specialist support is provided by BPI.

message: positioning / tagline: Logix Aurelia—a computer like no other. Your personal assistant in business.
positioning / academy message: Learn before you decide.
positioning / audience: Nontechnical business owners and managers; secondary audiences are dealers, software developers and peripheral manufacturers.

positioning / partner message: Business Tools organise office work; Abacus supports planning; independent BPI Systems maintains business records. Logix supplies the computer, not ownership of every application.
tagline: Logix Aurelia—a computer like no other. Your personal assistant in business.
claim_policy: Legacy acceptance wording (not new confirmation) / status: Accepted alternative-story plan; vendor contracts, measured demonstration performance and unspecified operating details remain execution gates.

acceptance gates / 0: Qualify 500-plus-row workload with stated RAM, populated-cell/formula count, IF and fill-down semantics, measured recalculation and disk loading time; sparse storage is not proof of performance.
acceptance gates / 1: Qualify powered-on attachment at quiescent ports, including electrical sequencing and safe suspension of keyboard polling; no unplugging during printing or disk writes.
acceptance gates / 2: Demonstrate save/close/reopen without loss; printer, disk and projection paths must pass the complete rehearsal.
acceptance gates / 3: Confirm celebrity/partner contracts, venue, Academy cities/course dates, tuition, product packages, delivery, warranty and service before publishing definitive claims.
acceptance gates / 4: Measured 48 KB workspace, disk capacity and supported disk configuration; 64 KB or extra drives only when qualified and separately quoted.
acceptance gates / 5: Posting consistency, correction history, disk-full handling and tested backup/restore.
acceptance gates / 6: Readable reports on launch display and supported printers; supported forms and paper documented.
acceptance gates / 7: Payroll jurisdictions, update process and maintenance responsibility explicitly documented.
acceptance gates / 8: Qualify BPI summary export and Abacus import; demonstrate actual sequential applications and label prepared data.

broadcast policy: Every Logix presentation at NCC 1978, including the premiere, both technical sessions, partner appearances, questions and any additional Logix sessions. Offer and supply the material free of charge to any television station wishing to broadcast it; Logix covers normal duplication and dispatch. Supply station-compatible broadcast copies on request.

stage.label: opening
stage.description: Adam introduces almost four years of development toward an accessible, dependable business assistant; acknowledges the assembled personal computers popularised in 1977.

stage.label: reveal
stage.description: Reveal one Aurelia platform with detachable keyboard and two display choices. Power on colour and 16-shade grayscale systems and show startup; no claim of two different CPU models.

stage.label: editing
stage.description: Prepare a customer quotation letter, demonstrate consistent editing and the copy-buffer; explain how learning transfers between applications.

stage.label: peripherals
stage.description: Attach the self-powered printer at a safely quiescent FlexiBUS port with Aurelia powered on, wait for identification, and print. Once the job finishes, safely interchange printer and keyboard ports and verify both. No removal during traffic or unrestricted hot-plug claim.

stage.label: business_tools
stage.description: Use address book, calendar and calculator in the same customer-order workflow.

stage.label: abacus
stage.description: Safely attach external FDD, load Abacus from diskette, explain a small worksheet, then open a 500-plus-row business document. Raise supplier costs by 8%, show automatic recalculation, add and fill a column using IF to flag low-margin orders, print a short report, save, close and reopen. Use readable worksheet sections on 320x200 launch displays. Use a labelled prepared worksheet with BPI-exported totals; explain their origin. The separate BPI session on 6 June shows the source records and export. Rehearse the shorter slot; retain the full workload for hands-on sessions.

stage.label: partners
stage.description: Gary explains independent CP/M OEM availability, published interfaces and optional extensions; CP/M, hardware and application licenses remain distinct. MPI explains the printer partnership and any separately agreed future FlexiBUS devices. Do not announce the later July SMC agreement. The head of BPI Systems explains its independent brand, management, software ownership and support, with Adam investment and AION/Logix cooperation disclosed. No invented name or claim of unrelated ownership.

stage.label: academy
stage.description: Announce Logix Computer Academy in five US cities: learn before you decide, hands-on Fundamentals, configuration advice, 50% tuition purchase credit and direct ordering. Show selected locations, first course dates and exact tuition once finalised. BPI-authorised courses and the dealer programme start July 17; specialist support is provided by BPI.

stage.label: packages
stage.description: State complete package contents and prices, delivery dates, warranty, training and service; invite orders, Academy registration and dealer demonstrations; announce the two technical sessions. Show optional dealer-assembled BPI configurations, separate supplier licences and training/setup prices.

before.title: Logix and DRI agree CP/M development for Aurelia
before.description: Building on the established DRI partnership, Logix and DRI agree a new CP/M version for Aurelia, fully owned by DRI and available to other vendors. Its development scope includes a text-mode TUI, Plug and Execute smart devices/cards over FlexiBUS, XIP cartridges and names for CP/M User Numbers.

inputs.description: The earlier DRI founding and funding milestone establishes the independent operating-system partner and relationship on which this CP/M collaboration is based.

outcomes.description: The agreed product is a new CP/M version for Logix Aurelia, fully owned by DRI and available for non-exclusive licensing to other vendors. Its scope includes XIP cartridges and named CP/M user areas; implementation and qualification follow this agreement.
The agreement establishes integration of the Logix TUI standard into the CP/M development scope: a consistent pseudo-window user interface in text mode for participating applications.

The agreement establishes CP/M integration work for FlexiBUS smart devices and expansion cards using Plug and Execute. This outcome covers agreed software support, not invention or completed manufacture of the underlying bus.

before.title: NCC 1982 — Pointy ideas with a solid point.
before.description: Introduce Color Pro 14 based on the February 1982 NEC PC-8853/JC-1410P2-class assembly, with AION digital-index/palette-to-RGB electronics and qualified 640x400 progressive Logix timing. New 64 KiB card retains previous features and adds 640x400x2 and 640x200x4; the remaining 1536 bytes hold up to 512 three-byte scanline palette entries. Horizontal and vertical retrace palette writes require explicit monitor capability and bounded timing. Launch the FlexiBUS two-button mouse with middle-finger vertical roller and thumb-side horizontal roller. Update AIONix and CP/M Platform Extensions/TUI to support pointing and standard-control activation without application source edits; statically linked libraries require relinking, and custom interfaces require adaptation. Release AION Entertainment Suite: Sudoku, Klondike Solitaire, Spider and FreeCell, with mouse-learning tutorials, keyboard alternatives and monochrome-compatible presentation. These titles and the dual-roller mouse are deliberate alternate-history offerings. June 7-10 Houston campaign: Pointy ideas with a solid point. Introducing the Logix Mouse. Point, select, and get to work. Colour business reports, hands-on mouse learning, partner compatibility demonstrations and professional graphics; AutoCAD remains a November target. Campaign plan and staged budget: ncc_1982_campaign.json.

outcomes.description: Demonstrate raster palette effects, unchanged standard-TUI controls with mouse input, and learning games. Keep later COMDEX high-resolution second-card/monitor plans separate; no unmeasured speed, cost or sales claims.

before.title: Aurelia+, Pulse, Abacus 2.0 and manufacturer compatibility kit arrive
before.description: Launches Aurelia+. Presents Pulse and Abacus 2.0. Makes corresponding training available. Launch the Aurelia Software Compatibility Kit with published contracts, reference runtime adapters, diagnostics and application acceptance tests. Manufacturers may independently implement the released environment; optional paid support and certification use standard terms. Application redistribution remains separately licensed. Shift new hardware development and promotion to Aurelia+ while enabling independent Aurelia-class clones. Continue installed-base support and compatible software; do not impose an immediate Aurelia withdrawal. FlexiBUS and Logix video adoption remain separate choices. compatibility policy / scope: Released Artemis application binaries using documented, supported ERA/AIONix interfaces retain a supported execution path on subsequent Logix professional platforms through 2000: native execution, a maintained compatibility runtime, or emulation. claims / memory: Beyond the 64 KB application barrier; demonstrate a measured resident workload on a named 128 KB or 256 KB configuration. Finite RAM and process limits remain; no demand paging promised.

claims / os: Professional multitasking AIONix with Unix V7-inspired behaviour and familiar Logix TUI/keyboard conventions. Do not claim a Unix source licence or trademark endorsement without an established agreement.

claims / compiler: Artemis-hosted AION C IDE supplies ERA native and Z80 cross-compilers, target libraries and separate executables. Portable code following guidelines can require small changes; quantify changes for each demonstration rather than promising zero work.

claims / applications: Native Abacus 2, Business Tools and qualified independent BPI editions. Pulse 1 remains Aurelia+ software; a card demonstration requires guest OS/memory qualification. Native Pulse 3 and Abacus 3 launch only at COMDEX on November 19.
claims / continuity: Aurelia+ remains a supported value option; compatible independent 8-bit computers grow the ecosystem. No forced migration or promise that cheaper 8-bit demand disappears.

video.mode_discovery: Enumerate controller modes intersected with identified or configured monitor raster capabilities and available buffering/sprite allocations. Reject unsupported downscaling.

memory_layout.mode_exclusivity: With palette-list mode enabled reserve 0xFA00–0xFFFF (1536 bytes); framebuffer/text/font allocations use 0x0000–0xF9FF. Text/font and bitmap layouts remain exclusive. Five sprites retain separate 1 KiB SRAM.
memory_layout.font_policy: One shared 256-glyph bank per mode. Font allocation 2048 bytes at 8×8, 4096 at 8×16 or 8×10 (16-byte glyph stride). Font writes affect both pages.

display_memory.organization: Two 16K x 16-bit banks; ordinary DRAM, not dual-port VRAM. Preserve independent refresh and bounded host access.

pixel_buffer.location: On video ASIC; SRAM banks with page ownership latches
pixel_buffer.policy: Eight-pixel parallel renderer fills free pages; independent clocked serializer drains ready pages. Two pages per 640-pixel line; prefill before active display; never overwrite displaying pages. Underflow blanks pixels, preserves sync and sets sticky fault.
pixel_buffer.physical_organization: Each 160-byte bank is 40 words × 32 bits. Load eight 4-bit pixels into a separate 32-bit serializer latch every eight dot clocks, then shift at 21.504 MHz. SRAM array reads run at 2.688 MHz, not one read per dot; filler and drain use different banks.

character_row_cache.purpose: Current and next 80-column character/attribute row; separate from 640-byte pixel FIFO.

timing_budget.qualification: Requalify existing renderer/FIFO and 16-bit DRAM organization for 640x400x2 and 640x200x4, refresh, sprite fetches, list prefetch and host/DMA stalls together. No greater upload throughput is promised by added capacity.

video.arbitration: Card-local sequencer arbitrates display fetch and deadline-reserved independent DRAM refresh before bounded host/DMA transfers with READY. Sprite SRAM has its own 8-bit bus. System DMA/MMU remain dedicated host components; the card does not replace system-memory refresh.

before.name: AIONix 2 (ERA² edition)
before.description: ROM-backed successor to AIONix: protected preemptive multitasking, documented ERA ABI compatibility, recoverable HDD storage, user access management and an event-driven TUI designed for later graphical windowing.

rom_execution.mapping: Shared read-only executable mappings; private writable data per process. Cacheable ROM with independently qualified timing.
rom_execution.physical_implementation: 256 KiB minimum system ROM bank; chip organization, package count, board mounting and timing remain qualification decisions.

compatibility.scope: Documented ERA AIONix user binaries, instruction semantics and C ABI; not Z80 binary compatibility.
compatibility.mechanism: Executable ABI version selects legacy adapters; stable library dispatch and capability discovery.
compatibility.limits: Undocumented kernel dependencies, privileged drivers and direct hardware access require separate qualification; portable Z80 C applications require recompilation.

multitasking.kernel: Compact monolithic kernel; timer-preempted user processes, bounded non-preemptible kernel critical sections.
requirements: Fair scheduling with priority aging
Sleeping I/O and atomic sleep/wakeup
Checked user pointers and protected kernel/device mappings
Process-exit cleanup of files, memory, locks and child state
Per-process memory, file and request limits
Driver timeouts and bounded retries
Short interrupt handlers with deferred work
Responsive administrative termination path
Kernel-controlled DMA with checked pinned buffers
multitasking.limits: Process isolation does not isolate kernel/driver faults or independently constrain DMA. Fully preemptible kernel and application threads are not initial requirements.

initial_target: Consistent open/read/write/close/lseek/stat and descriptor duplication, inheritance and errors
Reliable existing copy-on-write fork, exec, wait, exit status and environment
Defined signal delivery, masks, dispositions and interrupted-call semantics
Canonical/raw terminal modes, terminal attributes and foreground process groups
Hierarchical paths, working directories, hard links and symbolic links
Pipes with EOF/broken-pipe semantics and readiness multiplexing
Shell quoting, redirection, pipelines, variables and exit statuses
Wall clock, monotonic elapsed time and explicit timestamp formats
later: Efficient spawn without replacing fork semantics
Broader file control and memory mapping
Complete job control and pseudo-terminals
Sockets and additional IPC
Broader utilities, locales, threads and timers
posix_direction.conformance: Publish per-interface implemented/partial/absent matrix and unsupported-operation errors; names alone do not establish conformance.

filesystem.design: Versioned inode-based filesystem; directory entries separate from metadata.
filesystem.qualification_note: Testing range, not capacity ceiling or a change to bundled HDD sizes.
requirements: Direct and indirect block pointers
Ownership, permissions, link counts and timestamps
Bounded metadata/data cache
Mount support and logical-sector driver interface with CHS translation when required
Clean/dirty volume state and consistency checker
Ordered metadata writes and explicit synchronization
Backup/restore utilities and defined durable-save ordering
filesystem.later: Small metadata journal after write-order and power-loss testing; journal does not by itself guarantee application-data durability.

initial_target: Numeric users and groups
Owner/group/other read/write/execute and directory search permissions
Creation masks
Real/effective credentials
Login sessions and home directories
Protected password database with salted costed hashing selected against CPU budget
Administrative control of devices, mounts and configuration
Kernel enforcement on all relevant operations
Protected administrative audit records
user_access.privilege: Qualify credential and exec transitions before enabling set-user-ID programs. Server authenticates identity rather than trusting client-supplied UID.
user_access.later: Extended ACLs and more elaborate policies.

ui_layers.name: Application layer
ui_layers.responsibility: Business logic and semantic commands such as Open, Save, Select and Cancel, independent of rendering.

ui_layers.name: Abstraction layer
ui_layers.responsibility: Events, menus, forms, lists, focus, layout, text measurement and drawing contexts.

ui_layers.name: Translation and compatibility layer
ui_layers.responsibility: Existing TUI adapters, terminal rendering, device backends and legacy ABI behavior; later graphical renderers.

ui_layers.name: OS native API
ui_layers.responsibility: Processes, files, IPC, timers, input devices and controlled display access.

ui_contract.implementation: Logical layers primarily in shared libraries plus a small UI service; not four mandatory processes or IPC crossings. Extend the existing portable C API.
initial_target: Unified bounded event queue for keys, timers, focus, redraw and future pointer events
Semantic commands separated from physical keys
Opaque window/view handles initially representing text regions
Clipping, invalidation and repaint requests
Layout constraints and explicit text measurement
Separate cell and pixel coordinates
Bounded clipboard and selection ownership
Capability/version discovery for graphics, fonts, color and pointer input
ui_contract.memory: Compact text state, dirty regions and redraw callbacks; no mandatory full-screen RAM backing bitmap.
ui_contract.next_generation: Windowed GUI; legacy character applications run in terminal windows. Adapters do not automatically redesign old UIs.

memory_management.initial: Shared ROM code, sparse page tables, small kernel stacks, reliable copy-on-write and graceful allocation failure.
memory_management.later: Controlled disk-backed paging/swap only after restart, locking and I/O qualification; keep fault handlers and essential paging state resident.
memory_management.policy: Swap handles occasional pressure, not a routinely oversized working set; ROM does not replace writable RAM.

qualification: Measured ROM/RAM footprint and Abacus/compiler/server workloads
TUI capability fallback and legacy terminal behavior

priority_assessment.feasibility: Strong existing foundation; fit and patch behavior must be measured.
Feasible with ERA protection and restart rules; extensive verification.
20–100 MB addressing is straightforward; crash recovery is the main risk.
Feasible after process/filesystem isolation.
Phase interfaces; full contemporary conformance excluded.
Feasible groundwork; windowed GUI later.
Depends on proven faults and I/O; not initial release gate.

release_scope.initial: ROM execution, documented legacy ABI, protected preemptive processes, recoverable HDD storage, users/permissions, POSIX-oriented subset and event-driven TUI groundwork.
release_scope.later: Paging/swap, metadata journal, broader networking/threads/locales and full windowed GUI.

resource_planning.basis: Engineering allocation target, not a measured fit or maximum. Server retains its existing 1 MiB configuration.

distribution.execution: At least 256 KiB directly executable shared OS ROM, alongside at least 256 KiB DRAM. EEPROM BIOS remains boot/diagnostic firmware. Optional services, larger utilities and patches load from disk; do not copy the entire OS ROM into RAM.

memory.population_policy: Two matched 32-bit modules per capacity bank, selected independently on the 32-bit bus. Fill banks in order; all ranks require decoding and refresh. Cross-host connector/timing qualification pending.

os_rom.execution: Directly executable shared read-only AIONix2 code; private writable data and patch overlays in DRAM.
os_rom.implementation: System ROM bank; physical mounting, chip organization and access timing pending qualification.

video.mode_discovery: Enumerate controller modes intersected with identified or configured monitor raster capabilities and available buffering/sprite allocations. Reject unsupported downscaling.

memory_layout.mode_exclusivity: With palette-list mode enabled reserve 0xFA00–0xFFFF (1536 bytes); framebuffer/text/font allocations use 0x0000–0xF9FF. Text/font and bitmap layouts remain exclusive. Five sprites retain separate 1 KiB SRAM.
memory_layout.font_policy: One shared 256-glyph bank per mode. Font allocation 2048 bytes at 8×8, 4096 at 8×16 or 8×10 (16-byte glyph stride). Font writes affect both pages.
memory_layout.page_flip: Latch selected page during vertical blank; drawing throughput is not guaranteed by double buffering.

display_memory.organization: Two 16K x 16-bit banks; ordinary DRAM, not dual-port VRAM. Preserve independent refresh and bounded host access.

pixel_buffer.location: On video ASIC; SRAM banks with page ownership latches
pixel_buffer.policy: Eight-pixel parallel renderer fills free pages; independent clocked serializer drains ready pages. Two pages per 640-pixel line; prefill before active display; never overwrite displaying pages. Underflow blanks pixels, preserves sync and sets sticky fault.
pixel_buffer.physical_organization: Each 160-byte bank is 40 words × 32 bits. Load eight 4-bit pixels into a separate 32-bit serializer latch every eight dot clocks, then shift at 21.504 MHz. SRAM array reads run at 2.688 MHz, not one read per dot; filler and drain use different banks.

character_row_cache.purpose: Current and next 80-column character/attribute row; separate from 640-byte pixel FIFO.

timing_budget.qualification: Requalify existing renderer/FIFO and 16-bit DRAM organization for 640x400x2 and 640x200x4, refresh, sprite fetches, list prefetch and host/DMA stalls together. No greater upload throughput is promised by added capacity.

video.arbitration: Card-local sequencer arbitrates display fetch and deadline-reserved independent DRAM refresh before bounded host/DMA transfers with READY. Sprite SRAM has its own 8-bit bus. System DMA/MMU remain dedicated host components; the card does not replace system-memory refresh.
video.monitor_policy: All earlier modes and sprite/host/API features retained subject to monitor capabilities. Color Pro 14 and Mono Pro support the 640x400 raster; older displays retain their declared raster limits. Horizontal-retrace palette lists require explicit monitor capability; otherwise use static/vertical-retrace palette updates. No forced high scan rate on old monitors.

technical_profile.software_policy: Preserve documented ERA AIONix binaries through versioned compatibility; individual applications and editions require qualification. External application ROM cartridges are not added by the internal system ROM decision.

before.name: AIONix 2 (ERA² edition)
before.description: ROM-backed successor to AIONix: protected preemptive multitasking, documented ERA ABI compatibility, recoverable HDD storage, user access management and an event-driven TUI designed for later graphical windowing.

rom_execution.mapping: Shared read-only executable mappings; private writable data per process. Cacheable ROM with independently qualified timing.
rom_execution.physical_implementation: 256 KiB minimum system ROM bank; chip organization, package count, board mounting and timing remain qualification decisions.

compatibility.scope: Documented ERA AIONix user binaries, instruction semantics and C ABI; not Z80 binary compatibility.
compatibility.mechanism: Executable ABI version selects legacy adapters; stable library dispatch and capability discovery.
compatibility.limits: Undocumented kernel dependencies, privileged drivers and direct hardware access require separate qualification; portable Z80 C applications require recompilation.

multitasking.kernel: Compact monolithic kernel; timer-preempted user processes, bounded non-preemptible kernel critical sections.
requirements: Fair scheduling with priority aging
Sleeping I/O and atomic sleep/wakeup
Checked user pointers and protected kernel/device mappings
Process-exit cleanup of files, memory, locks and child state
Per-process memory, file and request limits
Driver timeouts and bounded retries
Short interrupt handlers with deferred work
Responsive administrative termination path
Kernel-controlled DMA with checked pinned buffers
multitasking.limits: Process isolation does not isolate kernel/driver faults or independently constrain DMA. Fully preemptible kernel and application threads are not initial requirements.

initial_target: Consistent open/read/write/close/lseek/stat and descriptor duplication, inheritance and errors
Reliable existing copy-on-write fork, exec, wait, exit status and environment
Defined signal delivery, masks, dispositions and interrupted-call semantics
Canonical/raw terminal modes, terminal attributes and foreground process groups
Hierarchical paths, working directories, hard links and symbolic links
Pipes with EOF/broken-pipe semantics and readiness multiplexing
Shell quoting, redirection, pipelines, variables and exit statuses
Wall clock, monotonic elapsed time and explicit timestamp formats
later: Efficient spawn without replacing fork semantics
Broader file control and memory mapping
Complete job control and pseudo-terminals
Sockets and additional IPC
Broader utilities, locales, threads and timers
posix_direction.conformance: Publish per-interface implemented/partial/absent matrix and unsupported-operation errors; names alone do not establish conformance.

filesystem.design: Versioned inode-based filesystem; directory entries separate from metadata.
filesystem.qualification_note: Testing range, not capacity ceiling or a change to bundled HDD sizes.
requirements: Direct and indirect block pointers
Ownership, permissions, link counts and timestamps
Bounded metadata/data cache
Mount support and logical-sector driver interface with CHS translation when required
Clean/dirty volume state and consistency checker
Ordered metadata writes and explicit synchronization
Backup/restore utilities and defined durable-save ordering
filesystem.later: Small metadata journal after write-order and power-loss testing; journal does not by itself guarantee application-data durability.

initial_target: Numeric users and groups
Owner/group/other read/write/execute and directory search permissions
Creation masks
Real/effective credentials
Login sessions and home directories
Protected password database with salted costed hashing selected against CPU budget
Administrative control of devices, mounts and configuration
Kernel enforcement on all relevant operations
Protected administrative audit records
user_access.privilege: Qualify credential and exec transitions before enabling set-user-ID programs. Server authenticates identity rather than trusting client-supplied UID.
user_access.later: Extended ACLs and more elaborate policies.

Separate cell and pixel coordinates

proposal.reason: Phase 4 catalogue cleanup under the current reference rules. Remove artificial-family and chip catalogue subjects; preserve the campaign scope in its existing title, messages and presentation. Consolidate genuine commercial promotion onto the retained offering; initial launch links remain later-phase work. Remove the internal 4164 chip from the launch subject list. Its system-memory role remains in the launch description and canonical hardware composition; the event does not market a separate RAM-chip offering. Describe the actual DRAM cost-review scope as an explained input against its base part, without adding future recipes or asserting a favourable review result. Remove the redundant chip product subject: the existing maturity outcome identifies the recipe, whose base_part_ids identify the DRAM. Preserve maturity stage, conditions and date exactly. Keep the direct Artemis launch prerequisite and the Academy/regional-office results. The narrative defines Artemis-line training scope without a family pseudo-product or a repeated top-level context link. Replace the Team Edition alias with the direct role of the retained package or its server/client implementations; no new separate offering or qualification success is inferred. Consolidate the initial-launch association onto the existing Team Edition package. Retain this explicit temporary exception until product launch links are assigned in the launch phase. Remove redundant chip product aliases from product_ids; the existing base_part_ids already identify exactly the manufactured silicon. Preserve recipe, qualification requirements and dated maturity assertions. Preserve the Artemis programme scope in its existing narrative and owned workstreams. Remove the family alias and repeated child software output from the parent summary; campaign ownership is already explicit in its steps. Keep the ecosystem scope in the narrative and direct predecessor inputs. Remove family and OS context lists rather than imply that this coordination process creates the platform or operating system. Remove the artificial-family and inherited campaign subject list from marketing execution. Preserve campaign messages, concrete activities and existing chronology; do not copy the catalogue into inputs or outputs. Qualify the actual Aurelia+ demonstration configuration rather than promote an internal memory-chip alias. The canonical computer composition retains its chip requirements. Remove duplicated package lists from the marketing execution process; the delivery process owns the package outcome and the event/campaign retain the unresolved launch association. Use canonical application implementations as the direct lineage inputs and explain the staged AIONix/Artemis target constraints. Preserve commercial product outcomes on the responsible delivery process. Keep the delivery process responsible for the one commercial package. Use canonical existing engineering resources and separate server/client qualification outputs; remove family and alias lists. Preserve the commercial meaning of the consolidated Team Edition aliases on the existing package; keep all composition lines, quantities, implementation versions and existing technical definitions unchanged. All removals and dependent reference revisions in this group must be reviewed atomically. Dates, ownership, technical BOMs, existing authorization and launch-link assignments are preserved. Approve its listed individual offering prerequisites first (or in the same batch) so reverse launch associations are removed only after equivalent product-owned links exist. AIONix preliminary work and its agreement refer to the canonical implementation; development hands that implementation to integration rather than creating an already released customer entitlement. Later graphics campaigns keep the operating-system demonstrations in their existing messages and owned events; remove the exchange-service subject because it does not describe that technical demonstration. before.title: Artemis platform launches commercially
before.description: Launch Artemis with AIONix, peripherals, expansions, developer tooling and support. Introduces Artemis training. At NCC 1980 reveal the processor architecture and word size withheld in the NCC 1979 public campaign. The separately sold Z80 compatibility module is an optional qualified legacy path; native applications require an appropriate target build. Released Artemis application binaries using documented, supported ERA/AIONix interfaces retain a supported execution path on subsequent Logix professional platforms through 2000: native execution, a maintained compatibility runtime, or emulation. Source portability is a separate commitment, not a substitute for the binary execution path. Demonstrate familiar multitasking, separate ERA/Z80 C builds and qualified legacy-card execution; compare verified vector calculations on Aurelia+, PDP-11/34 and Artemis before revealing the 32-bit RISC ERA 1 architecture. Publish only measured performance. The head of independent BPI Systems presents after Abacus and joins the partner section; BPI retains separate branding, licences, support and receipts. Ship Artemis 128 with a replaceable 16 KiB video card and Mono II or Color II; ship Artemis 256 with 32 AION 64 Kbit system RAM chips, a 32 KiB video card and Mono Pro or Color II. Both cards include 1 KiB exclusive sprite SRAM. Only the professional card and Mono Pro enable 640×400 modes; Color II keeps legacy timings. High-resolution demonstrations and paid follow-up campaign are separately budgeted; production qualification remains required. Logix introduced an Artemis 128 KiB office configuration with two floppy drives, a Color Monitor II, keyboard, AIONix, Business Tools and one year of support. A second configuration added a 5 MB disk subsystem. Customers could add Abacus 3 from November 1980 and networking from May 1981.

steps.description: AION Software and DRI began architecture, C portability and ERA operating-system work in February 1978.
Move the AIONix department from Copenhagen to Logix offices near DRI headquarters on 24 February 1978.
Milestone during this process: AIONix development programme and ownership formalised.
Following the September agreement, the teams developed the ERA operating system while maintaining CP/M and the Aurelia release line.
Complete the 12 October 1978 Logix share transfer. Gary’s 8% fulfils the AIONix promise; the other four 8% allocations remain the separately recorded contributor transfers.
Prepare confidential next-generation system software, application migration and C tools for Artemis without public disclosure before NCC 1980.
Complete this phase of AIONix development by 20 February 1980 and hand the work over for subsequent platform integration and commercial launch preparation. Ongoing maintenance continues separately.

before.title: Artemis platform launches commercially
before.description: Launch Artemis with AIONix, peripherals, expansions, developer tooling and support. Introduces Artemis training. At NCC 1980 reveal the processor architecture and word size withheld in the NCC 1979 public campaign. The separately sold Z80 compatibility module is an optional qualified legacy path; native applications require an appropriate target build. Released Artemis application binaries using documented, supported ERA/AIONix interfaces retain a supported execution path on subsequent Logix professional platforms through 2000: native execution, a maintained compatibility runtime, or emulation. Source portability is a separate commitment, not a substitute for the binary execution path. Demonstrate familiar multitasking, separate ERA/Z80 C builds and qualified legacy-card execution; compare verified vector calculations on Aurelia+, PDP-11/34 and Artemis before revealing the 32-bit RISC ERA 1 architecture. Publish only measured performance. The head of independent BPI Systems presents after Abacus and joins the partner section; BPI retains separate branding, licences, support and receipts. Ship Artemis 128 with a replaceable 16 KiB video card and Mono II or Color II; ship Artemis 256 with 32 AION 64 Kbit system RAM chips, a 32 KiB video card and Mono Pro or Color II. Both cards include 1 KiB exclusive sprite SRAM. Only the professional card and Mono Pro enable 640×400 modes; Color II keeps legacy timings. High-resolution demonstrations and paid follow-up campaign are separately budgeted; production qualification remains required. Logix introduced an Artemis 128 KiB office configuration with two floppy drives, a Color Monitor II, keyboard, AIONix, Business Tools and one year of support. A second configuration added a 5 MB disk subsystem. Customers could add Abacus 3 from November 1980 and networking from May 1981.

steps.description: AION Software and DRI began architecture, C portability and ERA operating-system work in February 1978.
Move the AIONix department from Copenhagen to Logix offices near DRI headquarters on 24 February 1978.
Milestone during this process: AIONix development programme and ownership formalised.
Following the September agreement, the teams developed the ERA operating system while maintaining CP/M and the Aurelia release line.
Complete the 12 October 1978 Logix share transfer. Gary’s 8% fulfils the AIONix promise; the other four 8% allocations remain the separately recorded contributor transfers.
Prepare confidential next-generation system software, application migration and C tools for Artemis without public disclosure before NCC 1980.
Complete this phase of AIONix development by 20 February 1980 and hand the work over for subsequent platform integration and commercial launch preparation. Ongoing maintenance continues separately.

proposal.title: Aurelia and Academy: concrete courses, operational sales and no family product
proposal.reason: Phase 4 catalogue cleanup under the current reference rules. Remove artificial-family and chip catalogue subjects; preserve the campaign scope in its existing title, messages and presentation. Consolidate genuine commercial promotion onto the retained offering; initial launch links remain later-phase work. The founding event creates the Academy organisation and prepares facilities. Course delivery and ordering operations belong to process.academy, not duplicate product placeholders. Identify the advertised before-you-buy service as the existing Fundamentals course. Preserve ordering and purchase-credit facts in the existing outcome; remove the sales-channel pseudo-product and unexplained prior-event subjects. The Academy process already owns the concrete course deliverables and stock-conditional ordering policy. Remove duplicate course-group and sales-channel products; avoid claiming later or unresolved services as launch deliverables. Remove the artificial-family and inherited campaign subject list from marketing execution. Preserve campaign messages, concrete activities and existing chronology; do not copy the catalogue into inputs or outputs. Preserve the before-you-buy interpretation on the existing two-day Fundamentals course without duplicating the course or altering its tuition, curriculum or purchase-credit policy. All removals and dependent reference revisions in this group must be reviewed atomically. Dates, ownership, technical BOMs, existing authorization and launch-link assignments are preserved. The course-location proposal now owns the Academy process and Fundamentals definition; approve it first or together so the duplicate-label removals preserve those definitions.

before.title: COMDEX 1979 campaign and presentation
before.objective: Communicate the launch, qualify demonstrations and coordinate follow-up described by the source campaign.
message: messages / campaign: More room to work. More freedom to choose.
messages / aurelia plus: Your existing software. Less waiting.
messages / abacus 2: Calculate once. Chart it. Print the documents.
claim_policy: Legacy acceptance wording (not new confirmation) / status: Accepted alternative-history campaign; demonstrations require qualification, not claimed measured results
partner policy / bpi: Independent branding, management, licences and support. The head of BPI speaks immediately after Abacus and joins the partner segment.
partner policy / peripherals: Demonstrate only individually qualified configurations. Invitations and targets are not agreements or shipments.

partner policy / manufacturers: Published interfaces and kit permit independent Aurelia-class implementations; support and certification optional. Native hardware adapters are valid; FlexiBUS and Logix video are separate profiles. Proper application/OS/firmware licences remain necessary.
commercial policy / new buyers: Clearly price hardware, required software and printing configuration; separately quote BPI licences and specialist setup.
commercial policy / existing owners: New capabilities for the computer you already own. Publish configuration requirements and explain workloads that benefit from Aurelia+.

commercial policy / manufacturers: Freely accessible specifications/self-tests, modest physical-kit pricing, optional bounded assistance and configuration-specific certification; no exclusive partnership required.
commercial policy / suppliers: Interoperability sessions and verified directory listings; document production supplies a concrete printer use case.
commercial policy / promotion: Prefer training, demonstration access and implementation help over another general price cut. Discounts, contracts and media spend are not invented.
strategy: Logix focuses new hardware development and promotion on Aurelia+ while enabling independent Aurelia-class clones and maintaining installed-base support; no immediate withdrawal date.

before.title: NCC 1979 open architecture and migration campaign
before.objective: Encourage independent manufacturers and developers to adopt documented compatibility interfaces, and show customers how supported software, documents and peripherals can protect their investment across computer brands.
audience: Business customers choosing computers, applications and peripherals.
Independent computer and peripheral manufacturers evaluating compatibility programmes.
Software publishers, developers, dealers and integrators supporting existing and future systems.
message: Choose your computer. Keep your investment.
Use documented interfaces and qualified configurations to connect products from independent suppliers.
Choose CP/M applications, FlexiBUS peripherals and display options separately; adopting one does not require the entire Logix platform.
Prepare for future computers through portable C source and documented interfaces while continuing to use and support established eight-bit systems.
claim_policy: Identify shipping products, qualified configurations, prototypes and plans separately. Manufacturer interest and campaign targets are not signed agreements, verified adoption or sales.

CP/M remains commercially licensed. Non-exclusive implementation rights do not make software free or open source, and final royalties, reference-code rights, certification fees and support terms must be stated before making firm offers.
Claim compatibility only for named software versions, resources, host adapters and tested configurations. Preserve each supplier’s brand, licences and support responsibilities.
Label the Model II demonstration as a prototype until customer release. AION supplies the June 1979 cards; SMC remains a future source subject to individual chip qualification.

Apple’s demonstration participation covers native Apple II products and does not endorse S-100 systems. These products provide neither Apple CP/M/Z80 execution nor automatic conversion of existing Apple graphics.

Until 19 May 1980, refer to future systems only as next-generation computers. Withhold product, processor and OS names; word size, ISA, registers, execution design, address and memory organisation; performance figures, clock rates, chip counts, schematics, board images, bus topology and future display specifications.

Keep coprocessor implementation and integration details, future-target SDKs, compiler output, binaries and revealing benchmarks confidential. Apply this embargo to presentations, questions, advertising, dealer scripts, sales proposals, OEM briefings, clinics and all attachments; current CP/M, FlexiBUS and optional display documentation may be shared.

Use released eight-bit software and explicitly identified qualified prototypes in demonstrations. Label prepared data and recordings, obtain partner clearance, and report measured resource and interoperability limits rather than implying universal performance.

Present Adam’s roughly ten-year price outlook as a strategic expectation, not an engineering guarantee, product withdrawal date or promise that every model remains in production. Do not promise funded support for an unspecified duration.

stage.label: Customer choice
stage.description: Explain how independent software, peripheral and display choices can protect a customer’s investment.

stage.label: Applications across computers
stage.description: Demonstrate an Abacus document round trip between Aurelia and the Model II prototype using separately qualified host editions. Show supported common behaviour without promising identical binaries or disk formats.

stage.label: Business applications
stage.description: Demonstrate Abacus, then independent BPI records and summary export. Explain the prepared data and separate licensing; do not imply that BPI has a Model II port.

stage.label: FlexiBUS peripherals
stage.description: Operate a qualified peripheral sequentially on named hosts. Show identification, driver support and supported application functions, attaching only when the port is quiescent.

stage.label: Apple II and S-100 expansion products
stage.description: Present the Apple II Expansion Card and FlexiDisk II alongside the S-100 FlexiBUS Interface, Apple II Video Card and S-100 Video Card. An Apple representative joins the native Apple demonstration. Explain the drivers, optional display hardware and separate S-100 support without suggesting Apple endorses S-100 systems.

stage.label: Independent partners
stage.description: DRI, Tandy, Microsoft, BPI management and confirmed peripheral participants explain their responsibilities and commercial access. Distinguish current AION chip supply from prospective SMC supply and signed partners from recruitment prospects.

stage.label: Preparing for the next generation
stage.description: Adam explains that future computers will not run existing Z80 binaries natively. Existing C tools and documented APIs reduce source migration work; recompilation, adaptation and testing remain necessary. Describe the planned optional Z80 coprocessor and the continuing role of eight-bit systems without revealing the new architecture.

stage.label: Availability and next steps
stage.description: Identify available products, prototypes and future plans. Direct customers and developers to documented configurations, licence terms, the compatibility directory and programme registration.

marketing_content.description: Specify the CP/M core and optional extension versions, processor instruction set, available transient-program memory, adapters and qualified applications for each configuration. Document common file formats and APIs. FlexiBUS and Logix video are optional; native displays, disks and conventional ports remain valid. Ordinary CP/M support does not guarantee every extended application, Z80 binary, file system or floppy format.

Publish electrical and transport rules, device-class profiles, host drivers, diagnostics and named qualification results. Other processors and operating systems may use their own drivers without adopting CP/M or Logix video. Device identification alone does not prove feature compatibility. Version 1 uses one device per point-to-point port, with no passive hub or daisy chain; its faster rate allows at most 50 KB/s before protocol overhead.

Separate graphics API compatibility from controller cards, the digital monitor link and qualified display modes. FlexiBUS and the full Aurelia architecture are optional. An 80-column mode needs a qualified 640-pixel monitor; adding a card does not give existing 320-pixel launch monitors that resolution.

marketing_content.type: Apple II and S-100 product sheet
marketing_content.description: The NCC launch covers the Apple II Expansion Card, FlexiDisk II, S-100 FlexiBUS Interface, Apple II Video Card and S-100 Video Card. The Apple II Expansion Card and FlexiDisk II are existing products presented alongside the three new interface/video cards. Cards initially use AION chips and include native Apple drivers and examples or supported S-100 CP/M adapters as appropriate. Keep host requirements and supplier support explicit.

Describe DRI’s software leadership and Logix’s hardware contribution. Invite independent computer, peripheral and software suppliers to a programme offering published specifications, versioning, backward-support policies, reference drivers, conformance tests, configuration diagnostics and a certification dispute process. Explain non-exclusive own-brand implementation, equal access to qualified components, disclosed supply priorities and manufacturer representation in a working group.

Identify the unresolved licence and royalty terms, reference-code redistribution rights, support duration and staffing, legacy-maintenance budget, working-group charter and voting rules, certification operator and fees, supply allocations, lead times and warranties. Present these as matters to settle, not existing contractual guarantees.

The 4 June 1979 announcement explains source migration and the planned optional Z80 compatibility path. Full architecture disclosure is scheduled for 19 May 1980. The all-years technical catalogue is internal author material, not a 1979 press kit.

Use the established Z80 C environment, documented APIs, portable file formats and separate platform adapters. A later target needs recompilation and testing, with review of assembly code, integer and pointer assumptions, memory banking and direct hardware access. Source portability does not preserve native Z80 binary execution.

Describe an optional Z80 coprocessor planned for qualified legacy applications. Availability and compatibility are not guaranteed for every model or hardware-dependent program. Keep its implementation, interconnect, memory mapping and host integration confidential until the architecture reveal.
Maintain CP/M tools and applications alongside next-generation development. Publish a funded support duration before making a dated service promise.
Explain that eight-bit computers retain useful business roles while falling costs broaden home, education and personal use. There is no fixed date when all business customers switch platforms.

From his 1979 perspective, Adam does not expect a next-generation computer using an existing television and basic storage to fall below roughly USD 100 for about a decade. The figure is nominal US retail pricing before tax, excluding a new screen and a complete disk-and-printer business configuration; the exact basic-storage allowance is unresolved. The current professional digital monitor interface cannot drive a consumer television, so such a product requires separate engineering and costing.

Invite suppliers to offer wider carriage, letter-quality printing, specialist forms and faster devices. Require the relevant status, character or graphics, paper and form-control support; the basic printer protocol does not cover every feature.
Invite business-chart and engineering-output devices, subject to a new plotting profile and suitable application support.
Invite communications and remote-access products with defined serial data, flow-control, modem-status and control profiles and host drivers.

Invite larger floppy systems, backup products and selected hard disks. Specify geometry, removable-media errors, durable writes, boot rules and measured throughput. Native faster disk controllers remain a valid choice.
Invite instruments, readers and business-input devices with published class or vendor-extension profiles and host drivers. Do not imply that foreign-processor ROM drivers execute automatically.

Document the actual file-transfer route and floppy formats used for the Aurelia-to-Model-II round trip. Publish tested RAM and application-workspace requirements, load and recalculation times and document-capacity limits. Label prepared data and recordings and preserve independent BPI branding and participant clearances.
Use booked presentation space; main-stage access, the exact slot and audiovisual suitability require confirmation. The eight presentation stages total 50 minutes, followed by questions.

Use this response to questions seeking confidential details: We will discuss the new architecture at NCC 1980. Today we can describe our C migration approach and planned optional Z80 compatibility path.

By the end of 1979, aim for Tandy shipping, one additional OEM selling a supported CP/M-extension or FlexiBUS configuration, another in qualification and verified third-party devices in several categories. By NCC 1980, aim for three to five distinct non-Logix manufacturers with supported configurations. Count Tandy once and exclude duplicate dealer builds and product variants; these are targets, not achieved results.

stage.description: DRI, Tandy, Microsoft, BPI management and confirmed peripheral participants explain their responsibilities and commercial access. Distinguish current AION chip supply from prospective SMC supply and signed partners from recruitment prospects.

stage.label: Preparing for the next generation
stage.description: Adam explains that future computers will not run existing Z80 binaries natively. Existing C tools and documented APIs reduce source migration work; recompilation, adaptation and testing remain necessary. Describe the planned optional Z80 coprocessor and the continuing role of eight-bit systems without revealing the new architecture.

stage.label: Availability and next steps
stage.description: Identify available products, prototypes and future plans. Direct customers and developers to documented configurations, licence terms, the compatibility directory and programme registration.

marketing_content.description: Specify the CP/M core and optional extension versions, processor instruction set, available transient-program memory, adapters and qualified applications for each configuration. Document common file formats and APIs. FlexiBUS and Logix video are optional; native displays, disks and conventional ports remain valid. Ordinary CP/M support does not guarantee every extended application, Z80 binary, file system or floppy format.

Publish electrical and transport rules, device-class profiles, host drivers, diagnostics and named qualification results. Other processors and operating systems may use their own drivers without adopting CP/M or Logix video. Device identification alone does not prove feature compatibility. Version 1 uses one device per point-to-point port, with no passive hub or daisy chain; its faster rate allows at most 50 KB/s before protocol overhead.

Separate graphics API compatibility from controller cards, the digital monitor link and qualified display modes. FlexiBUS and the full Aurelia architecture are optional. An 80-column mode needs a qualified 640-pixel monitor; adding a card does not give existing 320-pixel launch monitors that resolution.

marketing_content.type: Apple II and S-100 product sheet
marketing_content.description: The NCC launch covers the Apple II Expansion Card, FlexiDisk II, S-100 FlexiBUS Interface, Apple II Video Card and S-100 Video Card. The Apple II Expansion Card and FlexiDisk II are existing products presented alongside the three new interface/video cards. Cards initially use AION chips and include native Apple drivers and examples or supported S-100 CP/M adapters as appropriate. Keep host requirements and supplier support explicit.

Describe DRI’s software leadership and Logix’s hardware contribution. Invite independent computer, peripheral and software suppliers to a programme offering published specifications, versioning, backward-support policies, reference drivers, conformance tests, configuration diagnostics and a certification dispute process. Explain non-exclusive own-brand implementation, equal access to qualified components, disclosed supply priorities and manufacturer representation in a working group.

Identify the unresolved licence and royalty terms, reference-code redistribution rights, support duration and staffing, legacy-maintenance budget, working-group charter and voting rules, certification operator and fees, supply allocations, lead times and warranties. Present these as matters to settle, not existing contractual guarantees.

The 4 June 1979 announcement explains source migration and the planned optional Z80 compatibility path. Full architecture disclosure is scheduled for 19 May 1980. The all-years technical catalogue is internal author material, not a 1979 press kit.

Use the established Z80 C environment, documented APIs, portable file formats and separate platform adapters. A later target needs recompilation and testing, with review of assembly code, integer and pointer assumptions, memory banking and direct hardware access. Source portability does not preserve native Z80 binary execution.

Describe an optional Z80 coprocessor planned for qualified legacy applications. Availability and compatibility are not guaranteed for every model or hardware-dependent program. Keep its implementation, interconnect, memory mapping and host integration confidential until the architecture reveal.
Maintain CP/M tools and applications alongside next-generation development. Publish a funded support duration before making a dated service promise.
Explain that eight-bit computers retain useful business roles while falling costs broaden home, education and personal use. There is no fixed date when all business customers switch platforms.

From his 1979 perspective, Adam does not expect a next-generation computer using an existing television and basic storage to fall below roughly USD 100 for about a decade. The figure is nominal US retail pricing before tax, excluding a new screen and a complete disk-and-printer business configuration; the exact basic-storage allowance is unresolved. The current professional digital monitor interface cannot drive a consumer television, so such a product requires separate engineering and costing.

Invite suppliers to offer wider carriage, letter-quality printing, specialist forms and faster devices. Require the relevant status, character or graphics, paper and form-control support; the basic printer protocol does not cover every feature.
Invite business-chart and engineering-output devices, subject to a new plotting profile and suitable application support.
Invite communications and remote-access products with defined serial data, flow-control, modem-status and control profiles and host drivers.

Invite larger floppy systems, backup products and selected hard disks. Specify geometry, removable-media errors, durable writes, boot rules and measured throughput. Native faster disk controllers remain a valid choice.
Invite instruments, readers and business-input devices with published class or vendor-extension profiles and host drivers. Do not imply that foreign-processor ROM drivers execute automatically.

Document the actual file-transfer route and floppy formats used for the Aurelia-to-Model-II round trip. Publish tested RAM and application-workspace requirements, load and recalculation times and document-capacity limits. Label prepared data and recordings and preserve independent BPI branding and participant clearances.
Use booked presentation space; main-stage access, the exact slot and audiovisual suitability require confirmation. The eight presentation stages total 50 minutes, followed by questions.

Use this response to questions seeking confidential details: We will discuss the new architecture at NCC 1980. Today we can describe our C migration approach and planned optional Z80 compatibility path.

By the end of 1979, aim for Tandy shipping, one additional OEM selling a supported CP/M-extension or FlexiBUS configuration, another in qualification and verified third-party devices in several categories. By NCC 1980, aim for three to five distinct non-Logix manufacturers with supported configurations. Count Tandy once and exclude duplicate dealer builds and product variants; these are targets, not achieved results.

steps.description: Evaluate recruitment prospects and engineering kits. Prioritise North Star, with Lifeboat as a possible integration or distribution partner, then Vector Graphic. Preserve existing applications and display investment; interest does not constitute an agreement.

Treat North Star and Vector as strong CP/M prospects with moderately strong FlexiBUS prospects; optional Logix video is a moderate fit for North Star and a lower fit for Vector. Cromemco is a moderate CP/M and FlexiBUS prospect but a weak Logix-video prospect because of its own OS and graphics strategy. Altos is a moderately strong CP/M prospect with moderate FlexiBUS and limited Logix-video potential; no platform redesign is assumed. Intertec has moderately strong CP/M and moderate host-specific FlexiBUS potential, with limited Logix-video interest; plan late-1979 evaluation and possible 1980 qualification, not June availability. Heath/Heathkit has moderate CP/M and host-specific FlexiBUS potential but limited Logix-video interest; treat it as later feasibility work, not a promised 1979 release. These assessments guide outreach and do not establish commitments.
Publish compatibility profiles and provide reference-driver and test access alongside the separate DRI extension release. Record unresolved commercial and support terms.

Prepare the presentation space, audiovisual equipment and qualified demonstration systems. Test document round trips, disk formats, memory limits, loading, recalculation and device behaviour. Review all public material for the embargo and secure partner clearance.
Run supplier workshops, test named configurations and record failures and required corrections before public demonstrations.
Deliver the NCC presentation and the combined Apple II/S-100 expansion-product launch using the approved campaign materials and qualified systems.
Run dealer demonstrations, joint trade-press activity and developer clinics. Maintain a directory that distinguishes shipping, qualified and prototype configurations.
Update availability evidence for the separately recorded Tandy release and individually qualified SMC and peripheral products. Keep future products out of shipping claims.
Review progress against the campaign’s adoption targets using verified OEM configurations, qualifications and third-party device availability.

Track compatible-computer sell-through across vendors, qualified application editions, peripheral shipments and supported device classes, document-interchange results, support incidents, supplier concentration and component availability. Count distinct manufacturers rather than duplicate dealer builds or SKUs.

Prepare the closing review with verified customer examples, compatibility results and partner configurations. Report progress toward NCC 1980 goals without claiming unverified results or disclosing future architecture.

acceptance gates / 0: Qualify 500-plus-row workload with stated RAM, populated-cell/formula count, IF and fill-down semantics, measured recalculation and disk loading time; sparse storage is not proof of performance.
acceptance gates / 1: Qualify powered-on attachment at quiescent ports, including electrical sequencing and safe suspension of keyboard polling; no unplugging during printing or disk writes.
acceptance gates / 2: Demonstrate save/close/reopen without loss; printer, disk and projection paths must pass the complete rehearsal.
acceptance gates / 3: Confirm celebrity/partner contracts, venue, Academy cities/course dates, tuition, product packages, delivery, warranty and service before publishing definitive claims.
acceptance gates / 4: Measured 48 KB workspace, disk capacity and supported disk configuration; 64 KB or extra drives only when qualified and separately quoted.
acceptance gates / 5: Posting consistency, correction history, disk-full handling and tested backup/restore.
acceptance gates / 6: Readable reports on launch display and supported printers; supported forms and paper documented.
acceptance gates / 7: Payroll jurisdictions, update process and maintenance responsibility explicitly documented.
acceptance gates / 8: Qualify BPI summary export and Abacus import; demonstrate actual sequential applications and label prepared data.

broadcast policy: Every Logix presentation at NCC 1978, including the premiere, both technical sessions, partner appearances, questions and any additional Logix sessions. Offer and supply the material free of charge to any television station wishing to broadcast it; Logix covers normal duplication and dispatch. Supply station-compatible broadcast copies on request.

before.title: NCC 1979 open architecture and migration campaign
before.objective: Encourage independent manufacturers and developers to adopt documented compatibility interfaces, and show customers how supported software, documents and peripherals can protect their investment across computer brands.
audience: Business customers choosing computers, applications and peripherals.
Independent computer and peripheral manufacturers evaluating compatibility programmes.
Software publishers, developers, dealers and integrators supporting existing and future systems.
message: Choose your computer. Keep your investment.
Use documented interfaces and qualified configurations to connect products from independent suppliers.
Choose CP/M applications, FlexiBUS peripherals and display options separately; adopting one does not require the entire Logix platform.
Prepare for future computers through portable C source and documented interfaces while continuing to use and support established eight-bit systems.
claim_policy: Identify shipping products, qualified configurations, prototypes and plans separately. Manufacturer interest and campaign targets are not signed agreements, verified adoption or sales.

CP/M remains commercially licensed. Non-exclusive implementation rights do not make software free or open source, and final royalties, reference-code rights, certification fees and support terms must be stated before making firm offers.
Claim compatibility only for named software versions, resources, host adapters and tested configurations. Preserve each supplier’s brand, licences and support responsibilities.
Label the Model II demonstration as a prototype until customer release. AION supplies the June 1979 cards; SMC remains a future source subject to individual chip qualification.

Apple’s demonstration participation covers native Apple II products and does not endorse S-100 systems. These products provide neither Apple CP/M/Z80 execution nor automatic conversion of existing Apple graphics.

Until 19 May 1980, refer to future systems only as next-generation computers. Withhold product, processor and OS names; word size, ISA, registers, execution design, address and memory organisation; performance figures, clock rates, chip counts, schematics, board images, bus topology and future display specifications.

Keep coprocessor implementation and integration details, future-target SDKs, compiler output, binaries and revealing benchmarks confidential. Apply this embargo to presentations, questions, advertising, dealer scripts, sales proposals, OEM briefings, clinics and all attachments; current CP/M, FlexiBUS and optional display documentation may be shared.

Use released eight-bit software and explicitly identified qualified prototypes in demonstrations. Label prepared data and recordings, obtain partner clearance, and report measured resource and interoperability limits rather than implying universal performance.

Present Adam’s roughly ten-year price outlook as a strategic expectation, not an engineering guarantee, product withdrawal date or promise that every model remains in production. Do not promise funded support for an unspecified duration.

stage.label: Customer choice
stage.description: Explain how independent software, peripheral and display choices can protect a customer’s investment.

stage.label: Applications across computers
stage.description: Demonstrate an Abacus document round trip between Aurelia and the Model II prototype using separately qualified host editions. Show supported common behaviour without promising identical binaries or disk formats.

stage.label: Business applications
stage.description: Demonstrate Abacus, then independent BPI records and summary export. Explain the prepared data and separate licensing; do not imply that BPI has a Model II port.

stage.label: FlexiBUS peripherals
stage.description: Operate a qualified peripheral sequentially on named hosts. Show identification, driver support and supported application functions, attaching only when the port is quiescent.

stage.label: Apple II and S-100 expansion products
stage.description: Present the Apple II Expansion Card and FlexiDisk II alongside the S-100 FlexiBUS Interface, Apple II Video Card and S-100 Video Card. An Apple representative joins the native Apple demonstration. Explain the drivers, optional display hardware and separate S-100 support without suggesting Apple endorses S-100 systems.

stage.label: Independent partners
stage.description: DRI, Tandy, Microsoft, BPI management and confirmed peripheral participants explain their responsibilities and commercial access. Distinguish current AION chip supply from prospective SMC supply and signed partners from recruitment prospects.

stage.label: Preparing for the next generation
stage.description: Adam explains that future computers will not run existing Z80 binaries natively. Existing C tools and documented APIs reduce source migration work; recompilation, adaptation and testing remain necessary. Describe the planned optional Z80 coprocessor and the continuing role of eight-bit systems without revealing the new architecture.

stage.label: Availability and next steps
stage.description: Identify available products, prototypes and future plans. Direct customers and developers to documented configurations, licence terms, the compatibility directory and programme registration.

marketing_content.description: Specify the CP/M core and optional extension versions, processor instruction set, available transient-program memory, adapters and qualified applications for each configuration. Document common file formats and APIs. FlexiBUS and Logix video are optional; native displays, disks and conventional ports remain valid. Ordinary CP/M support does not guarantee every extended application, Z80 binary, file system or floppy format.

Publish electrical and transport rules, device-class profiles, host drivers, diagnostics and named qualification results. Other processors and operating systems may use their own drivers without adopting CP/M or Logix video. Device identification alone does not prove feature compatibility. Version 1 uses one device per point-to-point port, with no passive hub or daisy chain; its faster rate allows at most 50 KB/s before protocol overhead.

Separate graphics API compatibility from controller cards, the digital monitor link and qualified display modes. FlexiBUS and the full Aurelia architecture are optional. An 80-column mode needs a qualified 640-pixel monitor; adding a card does not give existing 320-pixel launch monitors that resolution.

marketing_content.type: Apple II and S-100 product sheet
marketing_content.description: The NCC launch covers the Apple II Expansion Card, FlexiDisk II, S-100 FlexiBUS Interface, Apple II Video Card and S-100 Video Card. The Apple II Expansion Card and FlexiDisk II are existing products presented alongside the three new interface/video cards. Cards initially use AION chips and include native Apple drivers and examples or supported S-100 CP/M adapters as appropriate. Keep host requirements and supplier support explicit.

Describe DRI’s software leadership and Logix’s hardware contribution. Invite independent computer, peripheral and software suppliers to a programme offering published specifications, versioning, backward-support policies, reference drivers, conformance tests, configuration diagnostics and a certification dispute process. Explain non-exclusive own-brand implementation, equal access to qualified components, disclosed supply priorities and manufacturer representation in a working group.

Identify the unresolved licence and royalty terms, reference-code redistribution rights, support duration and staffing, legacy-maintenance budget, working-group charter and voting rules, certification operator and fees, supply allocations, lead times and warranties. Present these as matters to settle, not existing contractual guarantees.

The 4 June 1979 announcement explains source migration and the planned optional Z80 compatibility path. Full architecture disclosure is scheduled for 19 May 1980. The all-years technical catalogue is internal author material, not a 1979 press kit.

Use the established Z80 C environment, documented APIs, portable file formats and separate platform adapters. A later target needs recompilation and testing, with review of assembly code, integer and pointer assumptions, memory banking and direct hardware access. Source portability does not preserve native Z80 binary execution.

Describe an optional Z80 coprocessor planned for qualified legacy applications. Availability and compatibility are not guaranteed for every model or hardware-dependent program. Keep its implementation, interconnect, memory mapping and host integration confidential until the architecture reveal.
Maintain CP/M tools and applications alongside next-generation development. Publish a funded support duration before making a dated service promise.
Explain that eight-bit computers retain useful business roles while falling costs broaden home, education and personal use. There is no fixed date when all business customers switch platforms.

From his 1979 perspective, Adam does not expect a next-generation computer using an existing television and basic storage to fall below roughly USD 100 for about a decade. The figure is nominal US retail pricing before tax, excluding a new screen and a complete disk-and-printer business configuration; the exact basic-storage allowance is unresolved. The current professional digital monitor interface cannot drive a consumer television, so such a product requires separate engineering and costing.

Invite suppliers to offer wider carriage, letter-quality printing, specialist forms and faster devices. Require the relevant status, character or graphics, paper and form-control support; the basic printer protocol does not cover every feature.
Invite business-chart and engineering-output devices, subject to a new plotting profile and suitable application support.
Invite communications and remote-access products with defined serial data, flow-control, modem-status and control profiles and host drivers.

Invite larger floppy systems, backup products and selected hard disks. Specify geometry, removable-media errors, durable writes, boot rules and measured throughput. Native faster disk controllers remain a valid choice.
Invite instruments, readers and business-input devices with published class or vendor-extension profiles and host drivers. Do not imply that foreign-processor ROM drivers execute automatically.

Document the actual file-transfer route and floppy formats used for the Aurelia-to-Model-II round trip. Publish tested RAM and application-workspace requirements, load and recalculation times and document-capacity limits. Label prepared data and recordings and preserve independent BPI branding and participant clearances.
Use booked presentation space; main-stage access, the exact slot and audiovisual suitability require confirmation. The eight presentation stages total 50 minutes, followed by questions.

Use this response to questions seeking confidential details: We will discuss the new architecture at NCC 1980. Today we can describe our C migration approach and planned optional Z80 compatibility path.

By the end of 1979, aim for Tandy shipping, one additional OEM selling a supported CP/M-extension or FlexiBUS configuration, another in qualification and verified third-party devices in several categories. By NCC 1980, aim for three to five distinct non-Logix manufacturers with supported configurations. Count Tandy once and exclude duplicate dealer builds and product variants; these are targets, not achieved results.
